entries.83480d821991e05de7cfd5d2bb0f7a4654dc1760: <div sID="gen3684" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="19" osisID="Deut.19" sID="Deut.19"/> <div eID="gen3684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3685" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen3686" type="x-p"/> The laws which Moses had hitherto been repeating and urging mostly concerned the acts of religion and devotion towards God; but here he comes more fully to press the duties of righteousness between man and man. This chapter relates, I. To the sixth commandment, "Thou shalt not kill," <reference osisRef="Deut.19.1-Deut.19.13">ver. 1-13</reference>. II. To the eighth commandment, "Thou shalt not steal," <reference osisRef="Deut.19.14">ver. 14</reference>. III. To the ninth commandment, "Thou shalt not bear false witness," <reference osisRef="Deut.19.15-Deut.19.21">ver. 15</reference>, &c.
entries.018e3ce4038178b5ff945683796c62c87ec1018d: <div eID="gen3686" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen3685" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Cities of Refuge. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1451.)</title> <div sID="gen3687" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> When the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God hath cut off the nations, whose land the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God giveth thee, and thou succeedest them, and dwellest in their cities, and in their houses; <hi type="super">2</hi> Thou shalt separate three cities for thee in the midst of thy land, which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God giveth thee to possess it. <hi type="super">3</hi> Thou shalt prepare thee a way, and divide the coasts of thy land, which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God giveth thee to inherit, into three parts, that every slayer may flee thither. <hi type="super">4</hi> And this <hi type="italic">is</hi> the case of the slayer, which shall flee thither, that he may live: Whoso killeth his neighbour ignorantly, whom he hated not in time past; <hi type="super">5</hi> As when a man goeth into the wood with his neighbour to hew wood, and his hand fetcheth a stroke with the axe to cut down the tree, and the head slippeth from the helve, and lighteth upon his neighbour, that he die; he shall flee unto one of those cities, and live: <hi type="super">6</hi> Lest the avenger of the blood pursue the slayer, while his heart is hot, and overtake him, because the way is long, and slay him; whereas he <hi type="italic">was</hi> not worthy of death, inasmuch as he hated him not in time past. <hi type="super">7</hi> Wherefore I command thee, saying, Thou shalt separate three cities for thee. <hi type="super">8</hi> And if the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God enlarge thy coast, as he hath sworn unto thy fathers, and give thee all the land which he promised to give unto thy fathers; <hi type="super">9</hi> If thou shalt keep all these commandments to do them, which I command thee this day, to love the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God, and to walk ever in his ways; then shalt thou add three cities more for thee, beside these three: <hi type="super">10</hi> That innocent blood be not shed in thy land, which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God giveth thee <hi type="italic">for</hi> an inheritance, and <hi type="italic">so</hi> blood be upon thee. <hi type="super">11</hi> But if any man hate his neighbour, and lie in wait for him, and rise up against him, and smite him mortally that he die, and fleeth into one of these cities: <hi type="super">12</hi> Then the elders of his city shall send and fetch him thence, and deliver him into the hand of the avenger of blood, that he may die. <hi type="super">13</hi> Thine eye shall not pity him, but thou shalt put away <hi type="italic">the guilt of</hi> innocent blood from Israel, that it may go well with thee. <div eID="gen3687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3688" type="x-p"/> It was one of the precepts given to the sons of Noah that <hi type="italic">whoso sheddeth man's blood by man shall his blood be shed,</hi> that is, by the avenger of blood, <reference osisRef="Gen.9.6">Gen. ix. 6</reference>. Now here we have the law settled between blood and blood, between the blood of the murdered and the blood of the murderer, and effectual provision made, <div eID="gen3688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3689" type="x-p"/> I. That the cities of refuge should be a protection to him that slew another casually, so that he should not die for that as a crime which was not his voluntary act, but only his unhappiness. The appointment of these cities of refuge we had before (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.13">Exod. xxi. 13</reference>), and the law laid down concerning them at large, <reference osisRef="Num.35.10-Num.35.15">Num. xxxv. 10</reference>, &c. It is here repeated, and direction is given concerning three things:— <div eID="gen3689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3690" type="x-p"/> 1. The appointing of three cities in Canaan for this purpose. Moses had already appointed three on that side Jordan which he saw the conquest of; and now he bids them, when they should be settled in the other part of the country, to appoint three more, <reference osisRef="Deut.19.1-Deut.19.3">v. 1-3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.19.7">7</reference>. The country was to be divided into three districts, as near by as might be equal, and a city of refuge in the centre of each so that every corner of the land might have one within reach. Thus Christ is not a refuge at a distance, which we must ascend to heaven or go down to the deep for, but the word is nigh us, and Christ in the word, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.8">Rom. x. 8</reference>. The gospel brings salvation <hi type="italic">to our door,</hi> and there it knocks for admission. To make the flight of the delinquent the more easy, the way must be prepared that led to the city of refuge. Probably they had causeways or street-ways leading to those cities, and the Jews say that the magistrates of Israel, upon one certain day in the year, sent out messengers to see that those roads were in good repair, and they were to remove stumbling-blocks, mend bridges that were broken, and, where two ways met, they were to set up a Mercurial post, with a finger to point the right way, on which was engraven in great letters, <hi type="italic">Miklat, Miklat—Refuge, Refuge.</hi> In allusion to this, gospel ministers are to show people the way to Christ, and to assist and direct them in flying by faith to him for refuge. They must be ready to remove their prejudices, and help them over their difficulties. And, blessed be God, <hi type="italic">the way of holiness,</hi> to all that seek it faithfully, is a highway so plain that <hi type="italic">the wayfaring men, though fools, shall not err therein.</hi> <div eID="gen3690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3691" type="x-p"/> 2. The use to be made of these cities, <reference osisRef="Deut.19.4-Deut.19.6">v. 4-6</reference>. (1.) It is supposed that it might so happen that a man might be the death of his neighbour without any design upon him either from a sudden passion or malice prepense, but purely by accident, as by the flying off of an axe-head, which is the instance here given, with which every case of this kind was to be compared, and by it adjudged. See how human life lies exposed daily, and what deaths we are often in, and what need therefore we have to be always ready, our souls being continually in our hands. How are the sons of men <hi type="italic">snared in an evil time, when it falls suddenly upon them!</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.12">Eccl. ix. 12</reference>. An evil time indeed it is when this happens not only to the slain but to the slayer. (2.) It is supposed that the relations of the person slain would be forward to avenge the blood, in affection to their friend and in zeal for public justice. Though the law did not allow the avenging of any other affront or injury with death, yet the avenger of blood, the blood of a relation, shall have great allowances made for the heat of his heart upon such a provocation as that, and his killing only, should not be accounted murder if he did it before he got to the city of refuge, though it is owned he was not worthy of death. Thus would God possess people with a great horror and dread of the sin of murder: if mere chance-medley did thus expose a man, surely he that wilfully does violence to the blood of any person, whether from an old grudge or upon a sudden provocation, must flee to the pit, and <hi type="italic">let no man stay him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.28.17">Prov. xxviii. 17</reference>); yet the New Testament represents the sin of murder as more heinous and more dangerous than even this law does. <reference osisRef="1John.3.15">1 John iii. 15</reference>, <hi type="italic">You know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him.</hi> (3.) It is provided that, if an avenger of blood should be so unreasonable as to demand satisfaction for blood shed by accident only, then the city of refuge should protect the slayer. Sins of ignorance indeed do expose us to the wrath of God, but there is relief provided, if by faith and repentance we make use of it. Paul that had been a persecutor obtained mercy, because he did it ignorantly; and Christ prayed for his crucifiers, <hi type="italic">Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.</hi> <div eID="gen3691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3692" type="x-p"/> 3. The appointing of three cities more for this use in case God should hereafter enlarge their territories and the dominion of their religion, that all those places which came under the government of the law of Moses in other instances might enjoy the benefit of that law in this instance, <reference osisRef="Deut.19.8-Deut.19.10">v. 8-10</reference>. Here is, (1.) An intimation of God's gracious intention to enlarge their coast, as he had promised to their fathers, if they did not by their disobedience forfeit the promise, the condition of which is here carefully repeated, that, if it were not performed, the reproach might lie upon them, and not on God. He promised to give it, <hi type="italic">if thou shalt keep all these commandments;</hi> not otherwise. (2.) A direction to them to appoint three cities more in their new conquests, which, the number intimates, should be as large as their first conquests were; wherever the border of Israel went this privilege must attend it, that <hi type="italic">innocent blood be not shed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.19.10">v. 10</reference>. Though God is the saviour and preserver of all men, and has a tender regard to all lives, yet the blood of Israelites is in a particular manner precious to him, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.14">Ps. lxxii. 14</reference>. The learned Ainsworth observes that the Jewish writers themselves own that, the condition not being performed, the promise of the enlarging of their coast was never fulfilled; so that there was no occasion for ever adding these three cities of refuge; yet the holy blessed God (say they) <hi type="italic">did not command it in vain, for in the days of Messiah the prince</hi> three other cities shall be added to these six: they expect it to be fulfilled in the letter, but we know that in Christ it has its spiritual accomplishment, for the borders of the gospel Israel are enlarged according to the promise, and in Christ, <hi type="italic">the Lord our righteousness,</hi> refuge is provided for those that by faith flee to him. <div eID="gen3692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3693" type="x-p"/> II. It is provided that the cities of refuge should be no sanctuary or shelter to a wilful murderer, but even thence he should be fetched, and delivered to the avenger of blood, <reference osisRef="Deut.19.11-Deut.19.13">v. 11-13</reference>. 1. This shows that wilful murder must never be protected by the civil magistrate; he bears the sword of justice in vain if he suffers those to escape the edge of it that lie under the guilt of blood, which he by office is the avenger of. During the dominion of the papacy in our own land, before the Reformation, there were some churches and religious houses (as they called them) that were made sanctuaries for the protection of all sorts of criminals that fled to them, wilful murderers not excepted, so that (as Stamford says, in his <hi type="italic">Pleas of the Crown, lib.</hi> II. <hi type="italic">c.</hi> xxxviii.) the government follows not Moses but Romulus, and it was not till about the latter end of Henry VIII's time that this privilege of sanctuary for wilful murder was taken away, when in that, as in other cases, the word of God came to be regarded more than the dictates of the see of Rome. And some have thought it would be a completing of that instance of reformation if the benefit of clergy were taken away for man-slaughter, that is, the killing of a man upon a small provocation, since this law allowed refuge only in case of that which our law calls chance-medley. 2. It may be alluded to to show that in Jesus Christ there is no refuge for presumptuous sinners, that <hi type="italic">go on still in their trespasses.</hi> If we thus <hi type="italic">sin wilfully,</hi> sin and go on in it, there <hi type="italic">remains no sacrifice,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.10.26">Heb. x. 26</reference>. Those that flee to Christ from their sins shall be safe in him, but not those that expect to be sheltered by him in their sins. Salvation itself cannot save such: divine justice will fetch them even from the city of refuge, the protection of which they are not entitled to.
entries.a10416378aaa642eed0a9672113deb0b52b0d1e5: <div eID="gen3693" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">False Witnesses. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1451.)</title> <div sID="gen3694" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> Thou shalt not remove thy neighbour's landmark, which they of old time have set in thine inheritance, which thou shalt inherit in the land that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God giveth thee to possess it. <hi type="super">15</hi> One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sinneth: at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established. <hi type="super">16</hi> If a false witness rise up against any man to testify against him <hi type="italic">that which is</hi> wrong; <hi type="super">17</hi> Then both the men, between whom the controversy <hi type="italic">is,</hi> shall stand before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , before the priests and the judges, which shall be in those days; <hi type="super">18</hi> And the judges shall make diligent inquisition: and, behold, <hi type="italic">if</hi> the witness <hi type="italic">be</hi> a false witness, <hi type="italic">and</hi> hath testified falsely against his brother; <hi type="super">19</hi> Then shall ye do unto him, as he had thought to have done unto his brother: so shalt thou put the evil away from among you. <hi type="super">20</hi> And those which remain shall hear, and fear, and shall henceforth commit no more any such evil among you. <hi type="super">21</hi> And thine eye shall not pity; <hi type="italic">but</hi> life <hi type="italic">shall go</hi> for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot. <div eID="gen3694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3695" type="x-p"/> Here is a statute for the preventing of frauds and perjuries; for the divine law takes care of men's rights and properties, and has made a hedge about them. Such a friend is it to human society and men's civil interest. <div eID="gen3695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3696" type="x-p"/> I. A law against frauds, <reference osisRef="Deut.19.14">v. 14</reference>. 1. Here is an implicit direction given to the first planters of Canaan to fix land-marks, according to the distribution of the land to the several tribes and families by lot. Note, It is the will of God that every one should know his own, and that all good means should be used to prevent encroachments and the doing and suffering of wrong. When right is settled, care must be taken that it be not afterwards unsettled, and that, if possible, no occasion of dispute may arise. 2. An express law to posterity not to remove those land-marks which were thus fixed at first, by which a man secretly got that to himself which was his neighbour's. This, without doubt, is a moral precept, and still binding, and to us it forbids, (1.) The invading of any man's right, and taking to ourselves that which is not our own, by any fraudulent arts or practices, as by forging, concealing, destroying, or altering deeds and writings (which are our land-marks, to which appeals are made), or by shifting hedges, meer-stones, and boundaries. Though the land-marks were set by the hand of man, yet he was a thief and a robber by the law of God that removed them. Let every man be content with his own lot, and just to his neighbours, and then we shall have no land-marks removed. (2.) It forbids the sowing of discord among neighbours, and doing any thing to occasion strife and law-suits, which is done (and it is very ill done) by confounding those things which should determine disputes and decide controversies. And, (3.) It forbids breaking in upon the settled order and constitution of civil government, and the altering of ancient usages without just cause. This law supports the honour of prescriptions. <hi type="italic">Consuetudo facit jus—Custom is to be held as law.</hi> <div eID="gen3696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3697" type="x-p"/> II. A law against perjuries, which enacts two things:—1. That a single witness should never be admitted to give evidence in a criminal cause, so as that sentence should be passed upon his testimony, <reference osisRef="Deut.19.15">v. 15</reference>. This law we had before, <reference osisRef="Num.35.30">Num. xxxv. 30</reference>, and in this book, <reference osisRef="Deut.17.6">ch. xvii. 6</reference>. This was enacted in favour to the prisoner, whose life and honour should not lie at the mercy of a particular person that had a pique against him, and for caution to the accuser not to say that which he could not corroborate by the testimony of another. It is a just shame which this law puts upon mankind as false and not to be trusted; every man is by it suspected: and it is the honour of God's grace that the record he has given concerning his Son is confirmed both in heaven and in earth by <hi type="italic">three witnesses,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.5.7">1 John v. 7</reference>. <hi type="italic">Let God be true and every man a liar,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.3.4">Rom. iii. 4</reference>. 2. That a false witness should incur the same punishment which was to have been inflicted upon the person he accused. <hi type="italic">If two, or three,</hi> or many witnesses, concurred in a false testimony, they were all liable to be prosecuted upon this law. (2.) The person wronged or brought into peril by the false testimony is supposed to be the appellant, <reference osisRef="Deut.19.17">v. 17</reference>. And yet if the person were put to death upon the evidence, and afterwards it appeared to be false, any other person, or the judges themselves, <hi type="italic">ex officio—by virtue of their office,</hi> might call the false witness to account. (3.) Causes of this kind, having more than ordinary difficulty in them, were to be brought before the supreme court, <hi type="italic">The priests and judges,</hi> who are said to be <hi type="italic">before the Lord,</hi> because, as other judges sat in the gates of their cities, so these at the gate of the sanctuary, <reference osisRef="Deut.17.12">ch. xvii. 12</reference>. (4.) There must be great care in the trial, <reference osisRef="Deut.19.18">v. 18</reference>. A diligent inquisition must be made into the characters of the persons, and all the circumstances of the case, which must be compared, that the truth might be found out, which, where it is thus faithfully and impartially enquired into, Providence, it may be hoped, will particularly advance the discovery of. (5.) If it appeared that a man had knowingly and maliciously borne false witness against his neighbour, though the mischief he designed him thereby was not effected, he must undergo the same penalty which his evidence would have brought his neighbour under, <reference osisRef="Deut.19.19">v. 19</reference>. <hi type="italic">Nec lex est justior ulla—Nor could any law be more just.</hi> If the crime he accused his neighbour of was to be punished with death, the false witness must be put to death; if with stripes, he must be beaten; if with a pecuniary mulct, he was to be fined the sum. And because to those who considered not the heinousness of the crime, and the necessity of making this provision against it, it might seem hard to punish a man so severely for a few words' speaking, especially when no mischief did actually follow, it is added: <hi type="italic">Thy eye shall not pity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.19.21">v. 21</reference>. No man needs to be more merciful than God. The benefit that will accrue to the public from this severity will abundantly recompense it: <hi type="italic">Those that remain shall hear and fear,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.19.20">v. 20</reference>. Such exemplary punishments will be warnings to others not to attempt any such mischief, when they see how he that <hi type="italic">made the pit and digged it has fallen into the ditch which he made.</hi>  <chapter eID="Deut.19"/> <div eID="gen3697" type="x-p"/>

entries.6d2fd568955c06bddc091349c873146a9a09a84d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1821"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 19</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Deut.19.1-Deut.19.13">De 19:1-13</reference>. Of the Cities of Refuge.</title> <div sID="gen2434" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1821"/><hi type="bold">2. Thou shalt separate three cities for thee in the midst of thy land--</hi>Goelism, or the duty of the nearest kinsmen to avenge the death of a slaughtered relative, being the customary law of that age (as it still is among the Arabs and other people of the East), Moses incorporated it in an improved form with his legislative code. For the protection of the unintentional homicide, he provided certain cities of refuge--three had been destined for this purpose on the east of Jordan (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.41">De 4:41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.35.11">Nu 35:11</reference>); three were to be invested with the same privilege on the west of that river when Canaan should be conquered.<div eID="gen2434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2435" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the midst of thy land--</hi>in such a position that they would be conspicuous and accessible, and equidistant from the extremities of the land and from each other. <div eID="gen2435" type="x-p"/>
entries.a52336fb8add0fec59197b5e0f85d3a89492028d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1822"/><div sID="gen2436" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1822"/><hi type="bold">3. Thou shalt prepare thee a way--</hi>The roads leading to them were to be kept in good condition and the brooks or rivers to be spanned by good bridges; the width of the roads was to be thirty-two cubits; and at all the crossroads signposts were to be erected with the words, Mekeleth, Mekeleth, "refuge, refuge," painted on them.<div eID="gen2436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2437" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">divide the coasts of thy land ... into three parts--</hi>the whole extent of the country from the south to the north. The three cities on each side of Jordan were opposite to each other, "as two rows of vines in a vineyard" (see on <reference osisRef="Josh.20.7">Jos 20:7</reference>). <div eID="gen2437" type="x-p"/>
entries.d44e24303d9b685f21ae3908efae637e8ece942d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1823"/><div sID="gen2438" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1823"/><hi type="bold">6-7. Lest the avenger of the blood pursue the slayer, while his heart is hot--</hi>This verse is a continuation of <reference osisRef="Deut.19.3">De 19:3</reference> (for <reference osisRef="Deut.19.4">De 19:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.19.5">5</reference>, which are explanatory, are in a parenthetical form), and the meaning is that if the kinsman of a person inadvertently killed should, under the impulse of sudden excitement and without inquiring into the circumstances, inflict summary vengeance on the homicide, however guiltless, the law tolerated such an act; it was to pass with impunity. But to prevent such precipitate measures, the cities of refuge were established for the reception of the homicide, that "innocent blood might not be shed in thy land" (<reference osisRef="Deut.19.10">De 19:10</reference>). In the case of premeditated murder (<reference osisRef="Deut.19.11">De 19:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.19.12">12</reference>), they afforded no immunity; but, if it were only manslaughter, the moment the fugitive was within the gates, he found himself in a safe asylum (<reference osisRef="Num.35.26-Num.35.28">Nu 35:26-28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.20.6">Jos 20:6</reference>). <div eID="gen2438" type="x-p"/>
entries.3c70e04a048c5a6ce0afc99e25d3ee26d1bbaaaa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1824"/><div sID="gen2439" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1824"/><hi type="bold">8-9. And if the Lord thy God enlarge thy coast--</hi>Three additional sanctuaries were to be established in the event of their territory extending over the country from Hermon and Gilead to the Euphrates (see <reference osisRef="Gen.15.18">Ge 15:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.23.31">Ex 23:31</reference>). But it was obscurely hinted that this last provision would never be carried into effect, as the Israelites would not fulfil the conditions, namely, "that of keeping the commandments, to love the Lord, and walk ever in his ways." In point of fact, although that region was brought into subjection by David and Solomon, we do not find that cities of refuge were established; because those sovereigns only made the ancient inhabitants tributary, instead of sending a colony of Israelites to possess it. The privilege of sanctuary cities, however, was given only for Israelites; and besides, that conquered territory did not remain long under the power of the Hebrew kings. <div eID="gen2439" type="x-p"/>
entries.9bd36890700a05c7174681fc90c60ec1f8b1701c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1825"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Deut.19.14">De 19:14</reference>. The Landmark Is Not to Be Removed.</title> <div sID="gen2440" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1825"/><hi type="bold">14. Thou shalt not remove thy neighbour's landmark, which they of old have set in thine inheritance--</hi>The state of Palestine in regard to enclosures is very much the same now as it has always been. Though gardens and vineyards are surrounded by dry-stone walls or hedges of prickly pear, the boundaries of arable fields are marked by nothing but by a little trench, a small cairn, or a single erect stone, placed at certain intervals. It is manifest that a dishonest person could easily fill the gutter with earth, or remove these stones a few feet without much risk of detection and so enlarge his own field by a stealthy encroachment on his neighbor's. This law, then, was made to prevent such trespasses. <div eID="gen2440" type="x-p"/>
entries.f6bfa4f4dbe7d497715a9c59db605709e8eba790: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1826"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Deut.19.15">De 19:15</reference>. Two Witnesses Required.</title> <div sID="gen2441" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1826"/><hi type="bold">15. One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity--</hi>The following rules to regulate the admission of testimony in public courts are founded on the principles of natural justice. A single witness shall not be admitted to the condemnation of an accused person. <div eID="gen2441" type="x-p"/>
entries.6f86c20bf647eee5a7c39cd090999f3fdd63eb70: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1827"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Deut.19.16-Deut.19.21">De 19:16-21</reference>. Punishment of a False Witness.</title> <div sID="gen2442" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1827"/>16-21. entries.1d63a4a352c01e1c0408f1fc7cba8049b6c1ddcd: <div eID="gen6821" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen6822" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6823" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6823" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6822" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6824" type="x-p"/> Three cities of refuge to be appointed in the midst of the promised land; the land being divided into three parts, a city is to be placed in each, a proper way to which is to be prepared, <reference osisRef="Deu.19.1-Deu.19.3">Deu 19:1-3</reference>. In what cases of manslaughter the benefit of those cities may be claimed, <reference osisRef="Deu.19.4-Deu.19.6">Deu 19:4-6</reference>. Three cities more to be added should the Lord enlarge their coasts, and the reasons why, <reference osisRef="Deu.19.7-Deu.19.10">Deu 19:7-10</reference>. The intentional murderer shall have no benefit from these cities, <reference osisRef="Deu.19.11-Deu.19.13">Deu 19:11-13</reference>. The landmark is not to be shifted, <reference osisRef="Deu.19.14">Deu 19:14</reference>. One witness shall not be deemed sufficient to convict a man, <reference osisRef="Deu.19.15">Deu 19:15</reference>. How a false witness shall be dealt with - he shall bear the punishment which he designed should have been inflicted on his neighbor, <reference osisRef="Deu.19.16-Deu.19.20">Deu 19:16-20</reference>. Another command to establish the lex talionis, <reference osisRef="Deu.19.21">Deu 19:21</reference>.
entries.efd61b3ff59658d377b2fb15583ca13529588002: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen6824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6825" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt separate three cities - See on <reference osisRef="Num.35.11">Num 35:11</reference> (note), etc.
entries.d6825328af8b8ad8ec07cffa93d0906946c0d379: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen6825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6826" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt prepare thee a way - The Jews inform us that the roads to the cities of refuge were made very broad, thirty-two cubits; and even, so that there should be no impediments in the way; and were constantly kept in good repair.
entries.68d66b2506330a385fd7281640fba061be48121d: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen6826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6827" type="x-p"/> Shalt thou add three cities more - This was afterwards found necessary, and accordingly six cities were appointed, three on either side Jordan. See <reference osisRef="Jos.21.1-Jos.21.3">Jos 21:1-3</reference>, etc. In imitation of these cities of refuge the heathens had their asyla, and the Catholics their privileged altars. See <reference osisRef="Exo.21.13">Exo 21:13</reference> (note), <reference osisRef="Exo.21.14">Exo 21:14</reference> (note), and <reference osisRef="Num.35.11">Num 35:11</reference> (note), etc.
entries.6408cb69abeed381e31c9aa06b78d2a1389b4e36: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen6827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6828" type="x-p"/> If any man hate his neighbor - See on <reference osisRef="Exo.21.13">Exo 21:13</reference> (note).
entries.fac95d12beee0eccadcae313bd9c82c1f4b0a37f: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen6828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6829" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt not remove thy neighbor's landmark - Before the extensive use of fences, landed property was marked out by stones or posts, set up so as to ascertain the divisions of family estates. It was easy to remove one of these landmarks, and set it in a different place; and thus the dishonest man enlarged his own estate by contracting that of his neighbor. The termini or landmarks among the Romans were held very sacred, and were at last deified. <div eID="gen6829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6830" type="x-p"/> To these termini Numa Pompillus commanded offerings of broth, cakes, and firstfruits, to be made. And Ovid informs us that it was customary to sacrifice a lamb to them, and sprinkle them with its blood: - <div eID="gen6830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6831" type="x-p"/> Spargitur et caeso communis terminus agno. <div eID="gen6831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6832" type="x-p"/> Fast. lib. ii., ver. 655. <div eID="gen6832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6833" type="x-p"/> And from Tibullus it appears that they sometimes adorned them with flowers and garlands: - <div eID="gen6833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6834" type="x-p"/> Nam veneror, seu stipes habet desertus inagris, <div eID="gen6834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6835" type="x-p"/> Seu vetus in trivio florida serta lap is. <div eID="gen6835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6836" type="x-p"/> Eleg. lib. i., E. i., ver. 11. "Revere each antique stone bedeck'd with flowers, <div eID="gen6836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6837" type="x-p"/> That bounds the field, or points the doubtful way." <div eID="gen6837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6838" type="x-p"/> Grainger. <div eID="gen6838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6839" type="x-p"/> It appears from Juvenal that annual oblations were made to them: - - Convallem ruris aviti <div eID="gen6839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6840" type="x-p"/> Improbus, aut campum mihi si vicinus ademit, <div eID="gen6840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6841" type="x-p"/> Aut sacrum effodit medio de limite saxum, <div eID="gen6841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6842" type="x-p"/> Quod mea cum vetulo colult puls annua libo. <div eID="gen6842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6843" type="x-p"/> Sat. xvi., ver. 36. "If any rogue vexatious suits advance <div eID="gen6843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6844" type="x-p"/> Against me for my known inheritance, <div eID="gen6844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6845" type="x-p"/> Enter by violence my fruitful grounds, <div eID="gen6845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6846" type="x-p"/> Or take the sacred landmark from my bounds, <div eID="gen6846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6847" type="x-p"/> Those bounds which, with procession and with prayer <div eID="gen6847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6848" type="x-p"/> And offer'd cakes, have been my annual care." <div eID="gen6848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6849" type="x-p"/> Dryden. <div eID="gen6849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6850" type="x-p"/> In the digests there is a vague law, de termino moto, Digestor. lib. xlvii., Tit. 21, on which Calmet remarks that though the Romans had no determined punishment for those who removed the ancient landmarks; yet if slaves were found to have done it with an evil design, they were put to death; that persons of quality were sometimes exiled when found guilty; and that others were sentenced to pecuniary fines, or corporal punishment.
entries.2450deee3c50f2e6adcec126d8653ce70c972c9a: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen6850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6851" type="x-p"/> One witness shall not rise up, etc. - See <reference osisRef="Num.35.30">Num 35:30</reference> (note).
entries.9e99acab41f1042c5e75ff0075743dee2c77a887: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen6851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6852" type="x-p"/> Then shall ye do unto him as he had thought to have done unto his brother - Nothing can be more equitable or proper than this, that if a man endeavor to do any injury to or take away the life of another, on detection he shall be caused to undergo the same evil which he intended for his innocent neighbor. <div eID="gen6852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6853" type="x-p"/> Some of our excellent English laws have been made on this very ground. In the 37th of Edw. III., chap. 18, it is ordained that all those who make suggestion shall incur the same pain which the other should have had, if he were attainted, in case his suggestions be found evil. A similar law was made in the 38th of the same reign, chap. 9. By a law of the twelve Tables, a false witness was thrown down the Tarpeian rock. In short, false witnesses have been execrated by all nations.
entries.7324d1bac21441943f2e23452c2b26c1baade679: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen6853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6854" type="x-p"/> Life - for life, eye for eye, etc. - The operation of such a law as this must have been very salutary: if a man prized his own members, he would naturally avoid injuring those of others. It is a pity that this law were not still in force: it would certainly prevent many of those savage acts which now both disgrace and injure society. I speak this in reference to law generally, and the provision that should be made to prevent and punish ferocious and malevolent offenses. A Christian may always act on the plan of forgiving injuries; and where the public peace and safety may not be affected, he should do so; but if law did not make a provision for the safety of the community by enactment against the profligate, civil society would soon be destroyed.  <chapter eID="Deut.19"/> <div eID="gen6854" type="x-p"/>

entries.01ef40e7f5da55548fa029bb7847be75b1c34de7: <reference osisRef="Deut.19.1-Deut.19.9">Deu 19:1-9</reference> <div eID="gen2379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2380" type="x-p"/> As Moses had already set apart the cities of refuge for the land on the east of the Jordan (Deu 4:41.), he is speaking here simply of the land on the west, which Israel was to take possession of before long; and supplements the instructions in Num 35:14, with directions to maintain the roads to the cities of refuge which were to be set apart in Canaan itself, and to divide the land into three parts, viz., for the purpose of setting apart these cities, so that one city might be chosen for the purpose in every third of the land. For further remarks on this point, as well as with regard to the use of these cities (<reference osisRef="Deut.19.4-Deut.19.7">Deu 19:4-7</reference>), see at Num 35:11. - In <reference osisRef="Deut.19.8-Deut.19.10">Deu 19:8-10</reference> there follow the fresh instructions, that if the Lord should extend the borders of Israel, according to His promise given to the patriarchs, and should give them the whole land from the Nile to the Euphrates, according to <reference osisRef="Gen.15.18">Gen 15:18</reference>, they were to add three other cities of refuge to these three, for the purpose of preventing the shedding of innocent blood. The three new cities of refuge cannot be the three appointed in Num 35:14 for the land on this side of the Jordan, nor the three mentioned in Num 35:7 on the other side of Jordan, as <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> and others suppose. Nor can we adopt Hengstenberg’s view, that the three new ones are the same as the three mentioned in <reference osisRef="Deut.19.2">Deu 19:2</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.19.7">Deu 19:7</reference>, since they are expressly distinguished from “these three.” The meaning is altogether a different one. The circumstances supposed by Moses never existed, since the Israelites did not fulfil the conditions laid down in <reference osisRef="Deut.19.9">Deu 19:9</reference>, viz., that they should keep the law faithfully, and love the Lord their God (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.4.6">Deu 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.6.5">Deu 6:5</reference>, etc.). The extension of the power of Israel to the Euphrates under David and Solomon, did not bring the land as far as this river into their actual possession, since the conquered kingdoms of Aram were still inhabited by the Aramaeans, who, though conquered, were only rendered tributary. And the Tyrians and Phoenicians, who belonged to the Canaanitish population, were not even attacked by David.
entries.dea1bd3fbb66e007bb857735fe7f0e86ca53aeb5: <reference osisRef="Deut.19.10">Deu 19:10</reference> <div eID="gen2380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2381" type="x-p"/> Innocent blood would be shed if the unintentional manslayer was not protected against the avenger of blood, by the erection of cities of refuge in every part of the land. If Israel neglected this duty, it would bring blood-guiltiness upon itself (“<hi type="italic">and so blood be upon thee</hi>”), because it had not done what was requisite to prevent the shedding of innocent blood.
entries.092582b692723fa0b7c3e911328407cd692b4f4c: <reference osisRef="Deut.19.11-Deut.19.13">Deu 19:11-13</reference> <div eID="gen2381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2382" type="x-p"/> But whatever care was to be taken by means of free cities to prevent the shedding of blood, the cities of refuge were not to be asyla for criminals who were deserving of death, nor to afford protection to those who had slain a neighbour out of hatred. If such murderers should flee to the free city, the elders (magistrates) of his own town were to fetch him out, and deliver him up to the avenger of blood, that he might die. The law laid down in Num 35:16-21 is here still more minutely defined; but this does not transfer to the elders the duty of instituting a judicial inquiry, and deciding the matter, as <hi type="italic">Riehm</hi> follows <hi type="italic">Vater</hi> and <hi type="italic">De Wette</hi> in maintaining, for the purpose of proving that there is a discrepancy between Deuteronomy and the previous legislation. They are simply commanded to perform the duty devolving upon them as magistrates and administrators of local affairs. (On <reference osisRef="Deut.19.13">Deu 19:13</reference>, see <reference osisRef="Deut.8.8">Deu 8:8</reference> and Deu 8:5.)
entries.8e339cdff85289c660d8ac538e746f5b8ba81d36: <reference osisRef="Deut.19.14">Deu 19:14</reference> <div eID="gen2382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2383" type="x-p"/> The prohibition against Removing a Neighbour’s Landmark, which his ancestors had placed, is inserted here, not because landmarks were of special importance in relation to the free cities, and the removal of them might possibly be fatal to the unintentional manslayer (as <hi type="italic">Clericus</hi> and <hi type="italic">Rosenmüller</hi> assume), for the general terms of the prohibition are at variance with this, viz., “thy neighbour’s landmark,” and “in thine inheritance which thou shalt inherit in the land;” but on account of the close connection in which a man’s possession as the means of his support stood to the life of the man himself, “because property by which life is supported participates in the sacredness of life itself, just as in <reference osisRef="Deut.20.19-Deut.20.20">Deu 20:19-20</reference>, sparing the fruit-trees is mentioned in connection with the men who were to be spared” (<hi type="italic">Schultz</hi>). A curse was to be pronounced upon the remover of landmarks, according to <reference osisRef="Deut.27.17">Deu 27:17</reference>, just as upon one who cursed his father, who led a blind man astray, or perverted the rights of orphans and widows (cf. Hos 5:10; <reference osisRef="Prov.22.28">Pro 22:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.23.10">Pro 23:10</reference>). Landmarks were regarded as sacred among other nations also; by the Romans, for example, they were held to be so sacred, that whoever removed them was to be put to death.
entries.5be6b843f96a44300e952e4ae745ed64220fbd14: <reference osisRef="Deut.19.15-Deut.19.16">Deu 19:15-16</reference> <div eID="gen2383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2384" type="x-p"/> The Punishment of a False Witness. - To secure life and property against false accusations, Moses lays down the law in <reference osisRef="Deut.19.15">Deu 19:15</reference>, that one witness only was not “to rise up against any one with reference to any crime or sin, with every sin that one commits” (i.e., to appear before a court of justice, or be accepted as sufficient), but everything was to be established upon the testimony of two or three witnesses. The rule laid down in <reference osisRef="Deut.17.6">Deu 17:6</reference> and Num 35:30 for capital crimes, is raised hereby into a law of general application (see at Num 35:30). קוּם (in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Deut.19.15">Deu 19:15</reference></hi>), to stand, i.e., to acquire legal force. - But as it was not always possible to bring forward two or three witnesses, and the statement of one witness could not well be disregarded, in <reference osisRef="Deut.19.16-Deut.19.18">Deu 19:16-18</reference> Moses refers accusations of this kind to the higher tribunal at the sanctuary for investigation and decision, and appoints the same punishment for a false witness, which would have fallen upon the person accused, if he had been convicted of the crime with which he was charged. סרה בּו לענות, “<hi type="italic">to testify against his departure</hi>,” sc., from the law of God, not merely falling away into idolatry (<reference osisRef="Deut.13.6">Deu 13:6</reference>), but any kind of crime, as we may gather from <reference osisRef="Deut.19.19">Deu 19:19</reference>, which would be visited with capital punishment.
entries.75c64a93530642a7d7ffa0e27b88f870aa5df1f3: <reference osisRef="Deut.19.17-Deut.19.20">Deu 19:17-20</reference> <div eID="gen2384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2385" type="x-p"/> The two men between whom the dispute lay, the accused and the witness, were to come before Jehovah, viz., before the priests and judges who should be in those days - namely, at the place of the sanctuary, where Jehovah dwelt among His people (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.17.9">Deu 17:9</reference>), and not before the local courts, as <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> supposes. These judges were to investigate the case most thoroughly (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.13.15">Deu 13:15</reference>); and if the witness had spoken lies, they were to do to him as he thought to do to his brother. The words from “<hi type="italic">behold</hi>” to “<hi type="italic">his brother</hi>” are parenthetical circumstantial clauses: “<hi type="italic">And, behold, is the witness a false witness, has he spoken a lie against his brother? Ye shall do,</hi>” etc. זמם, generally to meditate evil. On <reference osisRef="Deut.19.20">Deu 19:20</reference>, see Deu 13:12.
entries.dd8076e02d415e5a6772d65dae7df3a04e8b8487: <reference osisRef="Deut.19.21">Deu 19:21</reference> <div eID="gen2385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2386" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">lex talionis</hi> was to be applied without reserve (see at <reference osisRef="Exod.21.23">Exo 21:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.24.20">Lev 24:20</reference>). According to <hi type="italic">Diod. Sic.</hi> (i. 77), the same law existed in Egypt with reference to false accusers.  <chapter eID="Deut.19"/> <div eID="gen2386" type="x-p"/>

entries.f898599957cc20b8861ded5a9dc25b1e8b2c5d99:
1. When the Lord thy God hath cut off the nations. Moses repeats the same precepts which we have just been considering, that, in regard to murders, the people should distinguish between inadvertency and crime. With this view, he assigns six cities, wherein those who have proved their innocence before the judges should rest in peace and concealment. In one word, however, he defines who is to be exempt from punishment, viz., he who has killed his neighbor ignorantly, as we have previously seen; and this is just, because the will is the sole source and cause of criminality, and therefore, where there is no malicious feeling, there is no crime. But, lest under the pretext of inadvertency those who are actually guilty should escape, a mark of distinction is added, i.e., that no hatred should have preceded; and of this an instance is given, if two friends should have gone out together into a wood, and, without any quarrel or wrangling, the head of the axe should slip out of the hand of one of them, and strike the other. God, therefore, justly commands that the motive of the crime should be investigated, and shows how it is to be ascertained, viz., if there had been any previous animosity, or if any contention should have arisen. For it is incredible that any one should be so wicked as gratuitously to rush into so abominable a sin. It must be observed, however, that there was no room for this conjecture, except in a doubtful matter; for if any should stab his neighbor with a drawn sword, or should hurl a dart into his bosom, the inquiry would be superfluous, because the guilty intention would be abundantly manifest.

entries.2a339f27cb0a31d93dd4763dcea5287602829419:
A kind of theft is here condemned which is severely punished by the laws of Rome;
“In the digests there is a vague law, de termino moto, Digestor. Lib. 47. tit. 21, on which Calmer remarks, that, though the Romans had no determined punishment for those who removed the ancient land-marks, yet, if slaves were found to have done it with an evil design, they were put to death; that persons of quality were sometimes exiled when found, guilty; and that others were sentenced to primary fines, or corporal punishment. — Adam Clarke, in loco.
for that every one’s property may be secure, it is necessary that the land-marks set up for the division of fields should remain untouched, as if they were sacred. He who fraudulently removes a landmark is already convicted by this very act, because he disturbs the lawful owner in his quiet possession of the land;
“Est desia assez convaincu par ce seul acte d’avoir voulu debouter le possesseur de son champ;” is already sufficiently convicted by this act alone of having wished to deprive the possessor of his land. — Fr.
whilst he who advances further the boundaries of his own land to his neighbor’s loss, doubles the crime by the deceptive concealment of his theft. Whence also we gather that not only are those thieves, who actually carry away their neighbor’s property, who take his money out of his chest, or who pillage his cellars and granaries, but also those who unjustly possess themselves of his land.

entries.9fac608f01e3c9be3a42b157b4d27b7b0c4e604b:
16. If a false witness rise up against any man. Because the fear of God does not so prevail in all men, as that they should voluntarily abstain from the love of slander, God here appoints the punishment to be inflicted for perjury: for political laws are enacted against the ungodly and disobedient, in order that those who despise God’s judgment should be brought before the tribunal of men. Although perjury is not here ordained to be tried before the judges, unless there should be an accuser, who should complain that he had been unjustly injured by false-witness, still reason dictates, that if any man have been condemned to death by false-witnesses, the judges should not hesitate to make an official inquiry into the matter. Yet, inasmuch as men are generally disposed to assert their own innocence, God has deemed it sufficient to put the case, that if any complaint should be lodged, the judges should diligently investigate it, and if the crime be proved, should inflict the punishment of retaliation (talionis.) Whence it appears that false-witnesses and murderers stand in the same light before God. By commanding that the inquiry should be made not only by the judges, but also by the priests, as if God Himself were present, He shews that He requires unusual diligence to be used; because a secret crime is not easily detected without the most anxious care.
Tenth Commandment
Exodus 20
Exodus 20:17
17. Thou shalt not covet thy neighbor’s house, thou shalt not covet thy neighbor’s wife, nor his man-servant, nor his maid-servant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is thy neighbor’s.
17. Non concupisces domum proximi tui, non concupisces uxorem proximi tui, neque servum ejus, neque ancillam ejus, neque bovem ejus, neque asinum ejus, neque quicquam eorum quae sunt proximi tui.
ITS REPETITION
Deuteronomy 5

21. Neque concupisces uxorem proximi tui, neque concupisces domum proximi tui, agrum ejus, aut servum ejus, aut ancillam ejus, bovem ejus, aut asinum ejus: neque quicquam eorum quae sunt proximo tuo.
